title: Behavioral & STAR for Go Engineers — Revision

sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Behavioral interviews at Go engineering roles test how you handle ambiguity, conflict, failure, and growth. Interviewers want to hear Go-specific context: a story about migrating from a monolith to Go microservices, a conflict about when to add dependencies (Go philosophy: minimal stdlib), or a failure involving a goroutine leak or race condition in production. Generic answers score poorly; specific, technically grounded stories score high.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Every behavioral answer follows STAR: Situation (brief context), Task (your specific responsibility), Action (what you personally did—not 'we'), Result (measurable outcome). For Go engineers, actions should reference real tools and patterns: 'I added -race to the CI pipeline,' 'I refactored the handler to accept an interface so we could inject a mock,' 'I wrote an ADR explaining why we chose Go kit over a custom framework.' Results should include numbers: latency reduction %, error rate, lines of code removed, deployment frequency.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. STAR method: keep Situation + Task under 30 seconds; spend most time on Action and Result. 2. Conflict resolution: frame disagreements as technical trade-offs, not personality clashes; reference how you used data or a prototype to resolve it. 3. Failure stories: interviewers want to see self-awareness and learning; describe a real Go production issue (panic, data race, OOM), your diagnosis, and what you changed in process. 4. Migration stories: monolith to microservices, Python/Ruby to Go, GOPATH to modules—structure as before/after with metrics. 5. Leadership in Go teams: onboarding engineers to Go idioms, establishing code-review standards (golangci-lint config), writing ADRs for library choices.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: • 'Tell me about a time you improved system reliability.' → SLO definition, pprof investigation, graceful shutdown fix, error budget recovery. • 'Describe a technical disagreement you had.' → e.g., whether to use a framework vs. stdlib; how you built a prototype to compare; what the team decided. • 'Tell me about a production incident you caused.' → data race or goroutine leak; how you diagnosed it with pprof; what process change you introduced (goleak in tests, -race in CI). • 'How have you helped other engineers learn Go?' → idiomatic Go workshops, code-review templates, golangci-lint baseline configuration.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "Situation: We had a Go service that was leaking goroutines under load—runtime.NumGoroutine kept climbing and we'd hit OOM every few hours. Task: I was asked to diagnose and fix it within a sprint because we were two weeks from a major product launch. Action: I enabled the pprof goroutine endpoint and took profiles under production-like load. The flame graph showed thousands of goroutines blocked on a channel send in our event publisher—the consumer had silently stopped due to an unhandled context cancellation. I fixed the consumer to restart on cancellation and added goleak.VerifyNone to our test suite so future leaks are caught before merge. Result: Goroutine count stabilised, OOM restarts dropped to zero, and we shipped the launch on time. I also wrote an internal guide on goroutine lifecycle patterns that the team now references in code review."
